name: Chapter 15: Body Fluids and Circulation
description: Blood, blood groups, clotting, lymph, circulatory patterns, human heart, cardiac cycle, ECG, double circulation, disorders

cards.term: How do sponges and coelenterates move substances to cells?
cards.definition: They circulate water from surroundings through body cavities

cards.term: Two body fluids for transport in humans?
cards.definition: Blood and lymph

cards.term: Why is blood a connective tissue?
cards.definition:
It is a special connective tissue:
cells (formed elements) in a fluid matrix (plasma)
Originates from mesoderm

cards.term: What fraction of blood is plasma?
cards.definition: Nearly 55%
90–92% water 6–8% proteins minerals, glucose, amino acids, lipids, clotting factors
Straw coloured, viscous
Fibrinogen: Clotting of blood; Globulins: Defence (antibodies); Albumins: Osmotic balance

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Plasma proteins

Function?

FibrinogenClotting of blood
GlobulinsDefence (antibodies)
AlbuminsOsmotic balance

cards.definition: Plasma without clotting factors
Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻

cards.term: What are the formed elements, and what fraction of blood?
cards.definition: Erythrocytes, leucocytes, platelets; nearly 45%

cards.term: RBC count in a healthy adult man?
cards.definition: 5–5.5 million per mm³

cards.term: Where are RBCs formed in adults?
cards.definition: Red bone marrow

cards.term: Shape and nucleus of mammalian RBCs?
cards.definition: Biconcave, no nucleus in most mammals

cards.term: Why are RBCs biconcave and without a nucleus? (intuition)
cards.definition:
More surface area for gas exchange and more room for haemoglobin.
The thin shape lets them squeeze through capillaries
12–16 g

cards.term: Lifespan of RBCs, and where are they destroyed?
cards.definition: 120 days; destroyed in the spleen ("graveyard of RBCs")
They lack haemoglobin
6000–8000 per mm³

Neutrophils: 60–65% · phagocytic (most abundant); Lymphocytes: 20–25% · immunity (B and T); Monocytes: 6–8% · phagocytic; Eosinophils: 2–3% · resist infection, allergy; Basophils: 0.5–1% · histamine, serotonin, heparin; inflammation (least)

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Leucocytes

% of WBCs · role?

Neutrophils60–65% · phagocytic (most abundant)
Lymphocytes20–25% · immunity (B and T)
Monocytes6–8% · phagocytic
Eosinophils2–3% · resist infection, allergy

cards.definition: Most: neutrophils. Least: basophils.
Neutrophils and monocytes
Histamine, serotonin, heparin

cards.term: Which WBCs are associated with allergic reactions?
cards.definition: Eosinophils
"Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas": Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils
Cell fragments (thrombocytes) produced from megakaryocytes in bone marrow
1,50,000–3,50,000 per mm³

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints the platelet count as "1,500,00–3,500,00". Correct figure?
cards.definition: 1,50,000–3,50,000 per mm³ (150,000–350,000); the commas are misplaced in the book
Clotting disorders, excessive blood loss
ABO and Rh
Presence or absence of surface antigens A and B on RBCs
Antigens: chemicals that induce an immune response. Antibodies: proteins made in response to antigens.
A: A · anti-B · A, O; B: B · anti-A · B, O; AB: A, B · nil · AB, A, B, O; O: nil · anti-A, anti-B · O

cards.definition: Group O: RBCs carry no A or B antigen
Group AB: plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies
Clumping (agglutination) and destruction of RBCs

cards.term: Why is it called the Rh antigen?
cards.definition: It is similar to an antigen of Rhesus monkeys

cards.term: What percentage of humans are Rh+?
cards.definition: Nearly 80%

cards.term: What happens if an Rh− person receives Rh+ blood?
cards.definition: They form specific antibodies against Rh antigen

Rh− mother's anti-Rh antibodies destroy RBCs of an Rh+ foetus in a later pregnancy.
Result: severe anaemia, jaundice, even death

cards.term: Why is the first Rh+ baby usually safe?
cards.definition: The bloods are separated by the placenta; the mother is exposed to foetal blood only at delivery
Give anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the first delivery
To prevent excessive blood loss after injury

cards.term: What is a clot made of?
cards.definition: A network of fibrin threads trapping dead and damaged formed elements
Injury → platelets/tissues release factors → thrombokinase → prothrombin → thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin

cards.text: Thrombokinase converts {{c1::prothrombin}} to {{c2::thrombin}}, which converts {{c3::fibrinogen}} to {{c4::fibrin}}.

cards.term: Which ion is important in clotting?
cards.definition: Calcium (Ca²⁺)
It is an anticoagulant: prevents clotting inside vessels

Water and small solutes that leave capillaries into spaces between cells,
leaving large proteins and most formed elements behind
Same as plasma
Tissue fluid collected by the lymphatic system and drained back into major veins
Lymph: colourless, no RBCs, fewer proteins, has lymphocytes. Blood: red, RBCs, more proteins.
Carries specialised lymphocytes (immunity), nutrients and hormones; absorbs fats through lacteals

cards.term: Where are fats absorbed into lymph?
cards.definition: In the lacteals of intestinal villi
Blood flows from vessels into open spaces (sinuses); in arthropods, molluscs
Blood always flows in a closed network of vessels; in annelids, chordates

cards.term: Why is closed circulation more advantageous?
cards.definition: Flow can be regulated more precisely
Fishes: 2 (1 atrium, 1 ventricle) · single; Amphibians, reptiles: 3 (2 atria, 1 ventricle) · incomplete double; Crocodiles, birds, mammals: 4 (2 atria, 2 ventricles) · double

cards.definition: Crocodile (exception)

cards.term: Why is fish circulation called single?
cards.definition: Blood passes through the heart once per circuit; the heart pumps only deoxygenated blood to the gills

cards.term: Why is amphibian circulation incomplete double?
cards.definition: Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in the single ventricle

cards.term: Three parts of the human circulatory system?
cards.definition: A muscular chambered heart, closed branching blood vessels, and blood

cards.term: Germ layer origin of the heart?
cards.definition: Mesoderm

cards.term: Position and size of the heart?
cards.definition: In the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted left; size of a clenched fist
Double-walled pericardium enclosing pericardial fluid
Inter-atrial (thin, muscular), inter-ventricular (thick), atrio-ventricular (thick fibrous)
Tricuspid: right atrium → right ventricle (3 cusps). Bicuspid (mitral): left atrium → left ventricle.
"Try before you Buy": Tricuspid is on the right (comes first in the blood path), Bicuspid on the left
At the openings of the ventricles into the pulmonary artery and aorta

cards.term: Why are ventricle walls thicker than atrial walls?
cards.definition:
Ventricles pump blood to the lungs and whole body; atria only push blood next door.
The left ventricle is thickest.

cards.term: Figure 15.2 · Section of a human heart

cards.definition: Specialised cardiac musculature that is autoexcitable (generates action potentials without external stimuli)
Right upper corner of the right atrium
Lower left corner of the right atrium, near the atrio-ventricular septum
SAN → atria → AVN → AV bundle (bundle of His) → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres

cards.term: Why is the SAN called the pacemaker?
cards.definition: It generates the maximum number of action potentials (70–75/min), so it initiates and sets the rhythm

cards.term: Significance of the AVN and AV bundle?
cards.definition: They relay the impulse from atria to ventricles with a slight delay, so atria finish contracting first
70–75 beats per minute (average 72)
All four chambers relaxed; AV valves open, semilunar valves closed, blood fills ventricles

cards.term: How much does atrial systole add to ventricular filling?
cards.definition: About 30%

cards.term: Order of events in the cardiac cycle?
cards.definition:
1) Joint diastole
2) Atrial systole
3) Ventricular systole (AV valves close, semilunar open)
4) Ventricular diastole (semilunar close, AV open)
5) Joint diastole

cards.term: Why do the AV valves close during ventricular systole?
cards.definition: Rising ventricular pressure pushes blood back towards the atria, snapping them shut
The cyclically repeated sequence of systole and diastole of atria and ventricles
0.8 s (60 ÷ 72)
Blood pumped by each ventricle per cycle: about 70 mL
Stroke volume × heart rate: blood pumped by each ventricle per minute, about 5 L

cards.term: Why is an athlete's cardiac output higher?
cards.definition: The body can raise both stroke volume and heart rate

cards.term: What causes the first heart sound (lub)?
cards.definition: Closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves

cards.term: What causes the second heart sound (dub)?
cards.definition: Closure of the semilunar valves
Systole: contraction. Diastole: relaxation.
A graphical record of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle
Three: one to each wrist and one to the left ankle
Depolarisation of the atria → atrial contraction

cards.term: What does the QRS complex represent?
cards.definition: Depolarisation of the ventricles → ventricular contraction (starts shortly after Q)
Repolarisation of the ventricles; its end marks the end of systole

cards.term: How can heart rate be counted from an ECG?
cards.definition: Count the number of QRS complexes in a given time
P: atrial depolarisation. T: ventricular repolarisation.

cards.term: Why is atrial repolarisation not seen on an ECG?
cards.definition: It is hidden by the much larger QRS complex

cards.text:
Artery/vein wall: inner {{c1::tunica intima}} (squamous endothelium)
middle {{c2::tunica media}} (smooth muscle, elastic fibres)
outer {{c3::tunica externa}} (fibrous connective tissue, collagen).

cards.term: Which layer is thinner in veins?
cards.definition: Tunica media
Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium

Left ventricle
→ aorta

→ tissues
→ venules, veins, vena cava

cards.term: Which artery carries deoxygenated blood, and which vein oxygenated?
cards.definition: Pulmonary artery (deoxygenated); pulmonary vein (oxygenated)
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix, so tissues get fully oxygenated blood at high pressure

cards.term: What is the hepatic portal system?
cards.definition: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it reaches systemic circulation
Vessels exclusively for circulation to and from the cardiac muscle

cards.term: Why is the human heart called myogenic?
cards.definition: Its beat is initiated by specialised muscle (nodal tissue), not by nerves

cards.term: Where is the neural centre that moderates heart function?
cards.definition: Medulla oblongata, acting through the ANS

cards.term: Effect of sympathetic nerves on the heart?
cards.definition: Increase heart rate, strength of ventricular contraction and cardiac output

cards.term: Effect of parasympathetic nerves on the heart?
cards.definition: Decrease heart rate, conduction speed and cardiac output
Adrenal medullary hormones (adrenaline, noradrenaline)
120/80 mm Hg: systolic (pumping) / diastolic (resting)
Repeatedly 140/90 or higher
Heart diseases; affects vital organs like brain and kidney

Atherosclerosis:
deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrow arteries supplying the heart muscle
Acute chest pain when not enough O₂ reaches the heart muscle

cards.term: What is heart failure? Other name?
cards.definition: Heart not pumping effectively enough; congestive heart failure (lung congestion is a main symptom)

cards.term: Heart failure vs cardiac arrest vs heart attack
cards.definition: Heart failure: Pumps too weakly for body needs; Cardiac arrest: Heart stops beating; Heart attack: Heart muscle suddenly damaged by poor blood supply
